bib.title: Statistical Rethinking, Chapter 6: Overfitting, Regularization, and Information Criteria
bib.venue: book chapter (Statistical Rethinking: A Bayesian Course with Examples in R and Stan; CRC Press)

read.skipped: nothing; the PDF has no endnotes or reference list, so the footnote numbers (82-105) are unresolved

question: How should a modeller trade off simplicity against accuracy, i.e. avoid overfitting and underfitting, using regularizing priors and information criteria?
contributions: Explains overfitting and underfitting with the hominin polynomial example
Builds the target (out-of-sample deviance) from entropy, K-L divergence and deviance
Presents regularizing priors and AIC, DIC and WAIC as complementary tools
Shows model comparison and model averaging with Akaike weights

results.claim: R2 rises monotonically with polynomial degree; the 5th-degree fit reaches 0.99 and the 6th passes through all 7 points
results.setup: Hominin brain volume (cc) vs body mass (kg), 7 species, lm polynomials degree 1-6, flat priors
results.quote: The fifth-degree polynomial has an R2 value of 0.99!

results.setup: Hominin brain volume (cc) vs body mass (kg), 7 species, lm polynomials degree 1-6, flat priors

results.claim: 6th-degree polynomial has 7 parameters for 7 species, so fits perfectly (R2 = 1) and predicts negative brain size near 58 kg
results.setup: Hominin brain volume (cc) vs body mass (kg), 7 species, lm polynomials degree 1-6, flat priors
results.quote: At around 58 kg, the model predicts a negative brain size!

results.quote: the test deviance is smallest on average for 3 parameters

results.setup: Same simulation, flat priors, 10,000 sims per model
results.quote: Each distance is nearly twice the number of param-

results.claim: With the Normal(0,0.2) prior and N=20, models with 4 and 5 parameters are barely worse than the 3-parameter true model
results.setup: Same simulation with Normal(0,1), Normal(0,0.5), Normal(0,0.2) priors on betas; alpha not regularized; 10,000 sims
results.quote: the models with 4 and 5 parameters are barely worse than the correct model with 3 parameters

results.claim: At N=100 even Normal(0,0.2) is overwhelmed by the data; priors help little
results.setup: Same simulation, N=100
results.quote: there is enough information in the data to overwhelm even the Normal(0, 0.2) prior

results.claim: A Normal(0,1) prior on a standardized predictor gives only 5% plausibility to values beyond 2 SD
results.setup: Gaussian regularizing prior on a standardized slope
results.quote: assigns only 5% plausibility to values above and below 2 standard deviations

results.claim: AIC = Dtrain + 2p; valid only with flat priors, near-Gaussian posterior, N much greater than k
results.setup: Definition
results.quote: AIC = Dtrain + 2p

results.claim: DIC = Dbar + (Dbar - Dhat) = Dbar + pD; assumes multivariate Gaussian posterior and N >> k; reduces to AIC under flat priors
results.setup: Definition
results.quote: DIC = ¯D + (¯D −ˆD) = ¯D + pD

results.claim: WAIC = -2(lppd - pWAIC), pointwise, no Gaussian-posterior assumption, typically more accurate than DIC
results.setup: Definition
results.quote: WAIC = −2(lppd −pWAIC)

results.claim: DIC and WAIC estimates of out-of-sample deviance are within 1 point of actual average in most cases; WAIC more accurate
results.metric: error of IC vs mean test deviance
results.setup: 10,000 sims, models with 1-5 params, N=20, priors Normal(0,100) and Normal(0,0.5)
results.quote: being within 1 point of deviance of the actual average in most cases

results.claim: Regularization plus information criteria beat either alone (author's inference from Fig 6.11)
results.setup: Fig 6.11 simulation
results.quote: using both regularization and information criteria will always beat using only one or the other alone

results.note: Text says 'only 12 cases' (p200) but dim(d) is 17 rows and nobs=17 (p196, p202); also says 'more than 90% of the model weight'.

results.claim: Difference m6.14 vs m6.11 is 6.7 WAIC with dSE 7.26; simulated probability the difference is reversed is 0.1773
results.setup: Primate milk, Gaussian approximation of difference, 1e5 draws

results.setup: Primate milk compare table

results.claim: Akaike weight w_i = exp(-dWAIC_i/2)/sum_j exp(-dWAIC_j/2), read as probability of best prediction on new data, conditional on model set
results.setup: Definition
results.quote: A model’s weight is an estimate of the probability that the model will make the best predictions on new data, conditional on the set of models considered.

results.claim: WAIC standard error for the cars regression example is 14.43; WAIC 421.04
results.setup: cars data, dist ~ a + b*speed, 1000 posterior samples

limits: Information criteria are heuristics with no guarantees; assume test data come from the same process as training data (uniformitarian)
AIC needs flat priors, Gaussian posterior and N >> k; DIC needs Gaussian posterior; WAIC is hard to define for time series or dependent observations
IC are not consistent for identifying the true model
Akaike weights depend on the set of models compared; SE of WAIC is rough with small samples
No principled threshold of WAIC difference for 'significance'
Dated: uses first-edition rethinking package (map, map2stan, DIC); later editions replace with quap, ulam, PSIS-LOO and WAIC via compare; practice problems 6H1-6H6 have no printed solutions
practices: Do not choose among models by fit to sample (R2 or in-sample deviance), which always improves with parameters (p167-170).
Do not use p-value stargazing for model selection (p167, Rethinking: Stargazing).
Use regularizing priors on slopes of standardized predictors, tuned by cross-validation or information criteria (p186-188).
Use regularization and information criteria together; they are complementary (p194).
Fit all compared models to exactly the same observations; drop NAs first (p196).
Prefer model comparison and averaging over picking the lowest-WAIC model; retain and report all models (p195-196, p201).
Compare WAIC differences using dSE, not overlap of individual SEs (p199).
Compare parameter estimates across models as well as WAIC (p201).
Avoid trying every combination of predictors (Curse of Tippecanoe) (p204-205).
Standardize predictors before applying regularizing priors (p186).
Estimate log(sigma) to constrain sigma positive (p196-197).

terms.definition: poor prediction by learning too much from the data
poor prediction by learning too little from the data
a skeptical prior on a slope that slows the rate of learning from the sample; the same device as penalized likelihood
The reduction in uncertainty derived from learning an outcome.
H(p) = -sum p_i log(p_i): the average log-probability of an event (with a minus sign)
The additional uncertainty induced by using probabilities from one distribution to describe another distribution.
D(q) = -2 sum_i log(q_i), an approximation of relative K-L distance from the target
Dtrain + 2p, p = number of free parameters
Dbar + pD, pD = Dbar - Dhat, from the posterior distribution of training deviance
-2(lppd - pWAIC); pointwise, with lppd = sum log average likelihood and pWAIC = sum of variances of log-likelihood
w_i = exp(-0.5 dWAIC_i) / sum_j exp(-0.5 dWAIC_j)
using IC weights to build an ensemble posterior predictive distribution (prediction averaging)
selecting a model in which every coefficient is statistically significant
linear model with zero-centred Gaussian priors on slopes, precision lambda
